page: Amazon Web Services c8gb.12xlarge is an arm64 compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. It features 48 dedicated physical cores and 48 vCPUs powered by the ARMv9 AWS Neoverse-V2 processor clocked at 2.8 GHz, with 1 thread per core. The processor is backed by 64 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 36 MB of L3 cache, along with hardware AES support. The system delivers 96.0 GB of memory, allocating exactly 2.0 GB of RAM per core, along with a baseline network bandwidth of 100 Gbps. It does not include local instance storage or integrated GPUs.

Benchmark results demonstrate significant multi-threaded throughput and memory capabilities. The instance achieves top-tier results in Geekbench multi-core (23,775.0) and Clang software compilation (70,645.0), supported by strong stress-ng multi-core performance (81,853.63). Its memory subsystem registers top-tier metrics, including 407.39 GB/sec read and 196.56 GB/sec write bandwidth on large 256 MB blocks, alongside a top-tier PassMark memory score of 3,419.61. Single-core processing metrics, such as Geekbench single-core (1,896.0) and stress-ng single-core (1,706.58), place in the middle 50% tier.

Data serving and multi-threaded decompression tests emphasize its network and memory architecture. The platform delivers top-tier static web serving throughput of 98.05 GB/sec, top-tier PassMark database operations (47,511.48), and strong Redis SET throughput of 99.32 million operations per second. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression reaches 520.64 GB/sec. On LLM inference workloads, text generation for 7B and 70B models places in the top 25%, while small-model token generation falls in the lower quartile.

The 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio prioritizes core density and memory bandwidth over large RAM footprints. With dedicated cores and 100 Gbps networking, the server offers efficient compute distribution without thread contention. It is well-suited for distributed compilation pipelines, static web delivery, high-throughput network services, and containerized microservices requiring dedicated ARM compute.
